title: Blog 1
content:
Self-improving document processing with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Posted on: AWS Study Group VN (Facebook) – 06/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2328192347945724/
Figure: Architecture of the self-improving document processing solution with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Source: AWS Machine Learning Blog.
Traditional document processing usually needs templates, extraction rules and validation logic written for every document type. When a vendor changes an invoice layout, the system breaks, and old mistakes repeat because the system does not remember what was corrected before.
AWS presents a sample solution that tackles this with AI agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Main components:
Amazon Textract: extracts text from documents Strands Agents: open source SDK used to build the agent workflows S3 Vectors: stores embeddings (vectors that represent the meaning of text) to find similar documents EventBridge + Lambda: receive documents (by email or S3 upload) and create a processing job Amazon Bedrock: provides the Amazon Nova and Anthropic Claude models The solution has 8 agents working together in workflows:
Identification: finds the document type and sender, then looks for similar documents Training: generates extraction prompts, validates the result, fixes the prompts on failure and saves them Automation: for known document types, reuses the saved instructions to extract data The key idea is that learned instructions are reused later. In the post’s example, a repeated purchase order took 1 minute 30 seconds, compared with 3 minutes 49 seconds the first time. The estimated cost is about USD 58 per month for 10 training runs and 1,000 documents (US East).
Notes from the article:
The example uses synthetic data and a mock ERP, so real use needs your own schemas, validators and prompts The timings come from a single run and are not a benchmark Cost is mostly model inference (about 85%) Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is recommended for sensitive documents My takeaway: document processing is no longer just OCR followed by an LLM call. Agents can also learn from earlier corrections.
Source: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – AWS Machine Learning Blog (14/10/2026) https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/build-self-improving-document-processing-using-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/

Summary Report: “AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026” Event Information Event name: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 Date & time: Tuesday, 29/09/2026, 07:30 – 17:00 (UTC+7) Main venue: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi Where I attended: HCMC Watch Party – AWS Vietnam office, Ho Chi Minh City (live stream of the keynote and selected sessions) Role: Attendee Event page: https://aws.amazon.com/vi/events/cloud-day-hanoi/ Event Objectives Show how AWS helps builders turn ideas into real products with cloud and AI Introduce agentic AI (AI agents that can plan and carry out tasks) for developers, workload modernization and security Share real customer stories from Vietnamese companies Connect developers, IT leaders and the AWS community in Vietnam Keynote Speakers H.E. Jennifer Wicks – U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Dr. Werner Vogels – CTO, Amazon.com Eric Yeo – Country General Manager Malaysia, Vietnam, Indochina, AWS Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank Sessions I Attended Time Session Level 09:00 Keynote – What does it take to solve problems everyone says are impossible? (KEY001) 200 11:00 Building software like never before with agentic AI (DVT205 – HCMC Watch Party) 300 11:00 (Hanoi) Build an AI-ready data foundation (ANT202) / Migration at Scale with Agentic AI: AWS Transform and Beyond (AIM302) 200 / 300 Key Highlights Keynote: making “impossible” ideas possible AWS presented how its tools and resources help builders go beyond their limits, with experiences from customers such as Techcombank and Katalon. A big theme was agentic systems: AI agents that support developers, help modernize workloads and help keep organizations secure. Agentic AI for software development AI is moving from “suggesting code” to agents that can take a task, plan the steps and carry them out (write code, write tests, fix errors). The developer’s role shifts toward describing the problem clearly, reviewing the agent’s output and making the final decisions. AI-ready data foundation An AI application is only as good as its data: data needs to be collected, cleaned, organized and governed before it can be used by AI. The cloud provides managed services for storing and analyzing data so teams can focus on using it instead of maintaining infrastructure. Migration at scale with AWS Transform AWS Transform uses agentic AI to speed up migrating and modernizing large, old systems, a job that normally takes a lot of manual work. Key Takeaways AI is now a practical tool in real Vietnamese businesses, not just a research topic. Good AI starts with good data and a solid cloud foundation (security, cost control, monitoring). As an AI student, I need to learn both AI and cloud: models are only useful when they are deployed, monitored and secured in a real system. Applying to My Work Use the idea of an AI-ready data flow (upload → process → store → use) when designing our team’s capstone workshop. Prefer managed / serverless AWS services so the team can focus on the AI features instead of managing servers. Try AI coding assistants carefully: use them to speed up work, but always read and understand the generated code. Event Experience This was my first large AWS event. Watching the keynote and sessions together with other FCAJ interns at the HCMC Watch Party helped me see how cloud and AI are used by real companies in Vietnam. Many terms were new to me (agentic AI, data foundation, AWS Transform), so I noted them down to study further during the internship.

title: Blog 2
content:
Which vector store should you pick for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases? Posted on: AWS Study Group VN (Facebook) – 06/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2328194534612172/
When building RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) on Bedrock, the first question is where to store the vectors. The blog compares 3 options:
Amazon OpenSearch Service Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector Amazon S3 Vectors Each option is tested on a different use case:
Product search (OpenSearch): reducing vector dimensions from 1024 to 512 kept quality almost unchanged while the index shrank by nearly half (5.34 GiB to 2.79 GiB). Hybrid search (semantic plus keyword) improved quality by about 6%. Research agent (S3 Vectors): when the number of vectors grew 200 times (from about 5 thousand to about 1 million), p50 latency grew only about 3.5 times (82 ms to 294 ms). Customer-facing chatbot (Aurora PostgreSQL): with 500 thousand chunks, p50 latency was about 32 ms (HNSW), under 50 ms. The article’s suggestions:
Main need Suggested store Low latency (under 50 ms) and hybrid search OpenSearch Service Balanced, with relational data Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector Lowest cost at large scale, minimal operations S3 Vectors It also suggests a tiered design: S3 Vectors for the full corpus, and OpenSearch or Aurora for the performance-critical part.
Notes: the three tests used different datasets, so they cannot be compared head to head. They only show the shape of each trade-off. The latency numbers also exclude embedding generation time.
My takeaway: this article helps choose technology based on real needs instead of gut feeling.
Source: Selecting a vector store for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases – Deepak Dalakoti, Rhys Lewis, Petar Avramovic, AWS Machine Learning Blog (17/09/2026) https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/selecting-a-vector-store-for-amazon-bedrock-knowledge-bases/

title: Proposal
content:
ImageGuard – AI-Powered Image Moderation and Labeling on AWS Serverless Status: Proposal v2.0.
1. Overview ImageGuard is a serverless web application that helps classified-ad sites, forums and student clubs automatically moderate and categorize images uploaded by users. When a user uploads a photo, the system uses the computer-vision AI service Amazon Rekognition to:
Moderate: detect inappropriate content (violence, explicit content, weapons, drugs, …). Violating images are marked REJECTED and an administrator receives an email alert. Label: for valid images, automatically generate labels that describe the content (for example Laptop, Bicycle, Book) so users can search their images by label. Results are stored in Amazon DynamoDB and shown in the web UI within seconds. The whole system follows an event-driven, serverless architecture: there are no servers to manage, and the team pays only for actual usage.
2. Problem Statement Platforms that let users post images (classified ads, forums, community groups) receive many images every day. Manual review is labor-intensive and slow, and it exposes reviewers directly to harmful content. Without moderation, violating images can appear publicly and harm users and the platform’s reputation. User-uploaded images usually have no description or tags, so they are hard to find again. Solution: automate both tasks with AI as soon as an image is uploaded. Violating images are blocked before they are displayed; valid images are labeled for search.
3. Objectives & Scope 3.1. Objectives Build an automated pipeline, Upload → AI moderation → AI labeling → Storage → Display/Search, that runs entirely on AWS. Apply the AWS Well-Architected Framework, especially the Security pillar (IAM least privilege, no public resources, no hard-coded credentials). Provide full observability with Amazon CloudWatch (Logs, Metrics, Alarms) and email alerts through Amazon SNS. Keep operating cost at about USD 6–7/month under a realistic workload (Section 6). Write a bilingual step-by-step guide that lets others reproduce the deployment. 3.2. Success Criteria Criterion Target End-to-end processing time per image (upload → result) ≤ 10 seconds Violating images correctly blocked on the test set ≥ 90% Valid images wrongly blocked (false positives) on the test set ≤ 10% API calls without signing in Rejected (HTTP 401) User A reading User B’s images or results Not possible Violating image detected Email alert sent to the administrator Direct Internet access to S3 buckets Blocked (Block Public Access) 3.3. Scope In scope Out of scope JPG/PNG images, ≤ 5 MB Video, animated GIFs Content moderation + automatic labeling Face recognition (biometric data, privacy-sensitive) Label search within the user’s own images Full-text search across the whole system Sign-up/sign-in with Amazon Cognito Dedicated admin UI, appeals against moderation results Single Region: us-east-1 Multi-Region, disaster recovery 4. Solution Architecture Figure 1. ImageGuard architecture (drawn by the team in draw.io with the AWS Architecture Icons). Arrow numbers match the steps in Section 4.2.
4.1. AWS Services and Rationale Service Role in the system Why it was chosen Amazon S3 (1) Stores user images (private bucket); (2) hosts the static website 99.999999999% durability, low cost, emits S3 Events to trigger processing Amazon CloudFront Serves the static site over HTTPS and reads S3 through Origin Access Control (OAC) The website bucket stays private; free HTTPS; covered by the Always Free tier (1 TB/month) Amazon Cognito (User Pool) Sign-up, sign-in, issues JWT tokens Managed identity, free up to 10,000 MAU, the app never stores passwords Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) REST endpoints for the web app, protected by a Cognito JWT authorizer Cheaper than REST APIs (~USD 1 per million requests), native Cognito integration AWS Lambda (Python 3.12) Three functions: presign-upload, process-image, get-images Serverless, pay per invocation, scales automatically Amazon Rekognition DetectModerationLabels (moderation) and DetectLabels (labeling) Pre-trained AI, no model training needed; reads images directly from S3; available on the Free plan Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) Stores moderation results and labels per user Serverless NoSQL, pay per request, low latency, 25 GB free Amazon SQS Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) for failed processing events No data loss on failure; events can be reprocessed Amazon CloudWatch Logs, metrics (built-in + custom), alarms, dashboard Centralized monitoring, required by the workshop Amazon SNS Sends email when a violating image is found and when an alarm fires Simple; 1,000 emails/month free AWS IAM One dedicated least-privilege IAM role per Lambda function Security foundation of the whole system Why Region us-east-1: prices are usually the lowest among Regions and all required services are available. The ~200 ms latency from Vietnam has little impact, because the static site is served through CloudFront (with edge locations in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City) and the slowest step is AI image analysis anyway. For a real deployment serving Vietnamese users, the team would consider moving to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) to reduce latency and meet personal-data regulations; Region and resource names are environment variables, so no code changes are needed.
4.2. Data Flow The user opens the website through CloudFront, signs in with Cognito and receives a JWT token. The web app calls POST /upload-url on API Gateway with the token. API Gateway validates the token with the JWT authorizer and invokes the presign-upload Lambda. presign-upload creates a PENDING record in DynamoDB and returns a presigned URL (a temporary upload link that expires after 5 minutes) for the key uploads/{userId}/{imageId}.jpg. The browser uploads the image directly to S3 with the presigned URL, so the image never passes through Lambda or API Gateway. S3 emits an ObjectCreated event (only for the uploads/ prefix), which asynchronously invokes the process-image Lambda. process-image calls Rekognition DetectModerationLabels (Rekognition reads the image directly from S3): If a label from a blocked category is found with confidence ≥ 60%, the record is updated to REJECTED (with the reason) and an email is sent through SNS. Otherwise it calls DetectLabels (up to 10 labels, confidence ≥ 80%) and updates the record to APPROVED with the label list. If the Lambda still fails after 2 retries, the event is sent to the SQS DLQ. The web app calls GET /images?label=.... The get-images Lambda queries DynamoDB only by the userId taken from the token, filters by label if given, and returns the results. Images are displayed through short-lived presigned GET URLs, never made public. Every Lambda writes logs and metrics to CloudWatch; alarms send emails through SNS when errors occur. 4.3. Security Design (Security Pillar) Principle How ImageGuard applies it Least privilege Each Lambda has its own role. process-image may only call s3:GetObject on uploads/*, rekognition:DetectModerationLabels + rekognition:DetectLabels, dynamodb:UpdateItem on exactly one table and sns:Publish to exactly one topic. presign-upload may only call s3:PutObject on uploads/* and dynamodb:PutItem. get-images may only call dynamodb:Query and s3:GetObject Rekognition limitation Rekognition’s image-analysis APIs do not support resource-level permissions, so "Resource": "*" is required. The team compensates by allowing exactly the 2 actions needed, never rekognition:* No public resources Both buckets have Block Public Access enabled. The website bucket is readable only by CloudFront via OAC. The image bucket accepts and serves images only through short-lived presigned URLs Authentication & data isolation Every API requires a Cognito JWT. userId always comes from the token’s sub claim, never from client input, so users cannot read each other’s data No hard-coded credentials Lambdas use IAM roles (temporary credentials issued by AWS). Bucket, table and topic names are passed as environment variables. The GitHub repository contains no access keys and has a .gitignore Encryption S3 and DynamoDB encrypt data at rest by default; all traffic uses HTTPS/TLS Input protection Presigned URLs restrict the image Content-Type; the Lambda checks size (≤ 5 MB) and format before calling the AI Privacy No face recognition features are used; no biometric data is stored Why are the Lambdas not placed in a VPC/private subnet? The system has no database or server that needs a private network. The Lambdas reach S3, DynamoDB, Rekognition and SNS over HTTPS, authenticated by IAM. Putting them in a VPC would add NAT Gateway or interface VPC endpoint charges (tens of USD per month) without a meaningful security gain for this architecture. The team lists it as a future extension if compliance requires it.
4.4. Mapping to the AWS Well-Architected Framework Pillar Application Operational Excellence CloudWatch Logs (14-day retention), dashboard, alarms; a reproducible deployment guide Security See Section 4.3 Reliability Event-driven design; Lambda retries twice automatically; the DLQ keeps failed events; clear PENDING/APPROVED/REJECTED/FAILED states Performance Efficiency Direct-to-S3 uploads with presigned URLs; Rekognition reads images straight from S3 (the Lambda never downloads them); key-based DynamoDB queries Cost Optimization 100% serverless, pay per use; DetectLabels is called only after an image passes moderation; S3 Lifecycle; 14-day log retention; AWS Budgets Sustainability No idle resources; compute is used only when an image needs processing 4.5. Why Amazon Rekognition The initial plan used Amazon Bedrock for invoice processing. During testing, the team’s account had a Bedrock quota of 0, and the quota increase request was not approved. The team switched to Amazon Rekognition (a pre-trained AI service that is available on the current account and was tested successfully in the console) and kept most of the serverless architecture. The incident is documented in the Troubleshooting section of the workshop.
5. Plan & Timeline Internship period: 14/09/2026 – 04/12/2026. Planned workshop submission deadline: 19/11/2026 (15 days before the internship certificate is needed).
5.1. Roles Member Main responsibility Member A Team lead, integration, IAM & security Member B process-image Lambda, Rekognition integration, test image set and accuracy evaluation Member C Cognito, API Gateway, presign-upload and get-images Lambdas Member D Static web UI, S3 + CloudFront (OAC) Member E CloudWatch, SNS, DLQ, cost estimation, clean-up guide Every member must understand the whole architecture and be able to explain all of it, not only their own part.
5.2. Weekly Timeline Internship week Dates Tasks Output Week 7 26/10 – 01/11 Finalize topic, write proposal v1.0; test Bedrock, discover the zero quota Proposal v1.0, incident notes Week 8 02/11 – 08/11 Request a quota increase (denied); switch to Rekognition, write proposal v2.0; create S3, DynamoDB, IAM roles; build the process-image Lambda + S3 event Proposal v2.0, working image pipeline Week 9 09/11 – 15/11 Cognito, API Gateway, the two API Lambdas; static site + CloudFront; CloudWatch metrics/alarms/dashboard, SNS, DLQ; testing; AWS Pricing Calculator; record the demo video End-to-end demo, video, cost table Week 10 16/11 – 19/11 Write the bilingual 5-Workshop section (step-by-step, testing, clean-up), take screenshots, finalize the diagram, peer review Submit workshop on 19/11 Week 10–12 20/11 – 04/12 Apply mentor feedback, finish blogs and worklogs, clean up resources Final report 6. Cost Estimation Workload scenario: a small forum/classified-ad site receives about 3,000 images/month (~100/day), 1 MB on average, about 3% violating, and about 30,000 views/searches per month. Region us-east-1, on-demand prices, before Free Tier/credits.
Service Assumptions Estimated cost (USD/month) Amazon Rekognition 3,000 DetectModerationLabels + ~2,910 DetectLabels calls × USD 0.001/image 5.91 AWS Lambda 36,000 invocations, ~3,200 GB-seconds 0.06 (within the free tier) Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) 33,000 requests 0.03 Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) ~6,000 WRU + 30,000 RRU, < 1 GB 0.01 Amazon S3 3 GB (30-day lifecycle), 3,000 PUT, 6,000 GET 0.09 Amazon CloudWatch 0.5 GB logs, 3 alarms, 3 custom metrics, 1 dashboard 0.27 (mostly within the free tier) Amazon CloudFront ~2 GB transfer, 40,000 requests 0.00 (Always Free) Amazon Cognito < 10,000 MAU 0.00 Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS About 100 emails/messages 0.00 Total ≈ USD 6.40/month (≈ USD 76/year) During development and the demo (fewer than 300 images expected), Rekognition costs only about USD 0.60, and everything is covered by the account’s credits.
AWS Pricing Calculator link: [to be added after the estimate is created]
Cost Optimization Strategy 100% serverless architecture: no EC2, NAT Gateway or always-on resources. Moderate first, label second: violating images skip DetectLabels, saving one API call per blocked image. Rekognition reads images directly from S3, so the Lambda runs briefly (~2 seconds) with little memory (256 MB). S3 Lifecycle policy deletes images after 30 days (or moves them to S3 Glacier if long-term retention is needed). 14-day CloudWatch Logs retention instead of the default “Never expire”. HTTP API instead of REST API (about 70% cheaper). AWS Budgets alert at USD 10; run the clean-up right after grading. Above 1 million images/month, Rekognition’s tiered pricing lowers the per-image cost automatically. 7. Risks & Mitigation Risk Impact Mitigation Rekognition blocks valid images or misses violating ones Poor user experience or harmful content slips through Confidence threshold and blocked categories are environment variables that can be tuned; accuracy measured on the test set Service quotas on new accounts (already happened with Bedrock) AI calls fail Rekognition verified to work on the account; retry with backoff on throttling Recursive S3 → Lambda → S3 trigger Runaway cost Trigger only on the uploads/ prefix; the Lambda never writes back to S3 Access keys leaked to GitHub Account compromise Use IAM roles only; .gitignore; review before every commit Test images that infringe copyright or are too disturbing Legal and ethical issues Use the team’s own photos or freely licensed images; test moderation with mild categories (alcohol, tobacco, toy weapons) Unexpected charges Credit loss AWS Budgets; clean-up checklist Limited time (~2 weeks) Missing the deadline Build the MVP first, extras later; every week has a clear deliverable Members are still new to AWS Delays; cannot answer the mentor’s questions Learn while building; peer reviews; every member explains the full architecture 8. Expected Outcomes A working web application: sign in → upload an image → violating images are blocked with an email alert, valid images are labeled and searchable. A monitoring setup with a CloudWatch dashboard, alarms and email alerts. A bilingual workshop guide that can be reproduced from scratch, including testing, troubleshooting and clean-up. Hands-on skills for the team: event-driven serverless architecture, IAM least privilege, AWS AI services, monitoring and cost optimization, and how to adapt when a service is quota-restricted.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: “FCAJ Community Day” Event Information Event name: FCAJ Community Day Date & time: Saturday, 31/10/2026, 09:00 – 12:00 Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Sai Gon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Attendee Event page: https://luma.com/1izeyind Event Objectives Share real experience from building software and using AWS services in practice Help students understand what the cloud industry expects and how to prepare Introduce new ways of building serverless and asynchronous systems on AWS Encourage interns to contribute to open source and learn from the community Agenda Time Session 09:00 – 09:25 Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories 09:30 – 09:55 Education 10:00 – 10:25 AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture 10:30 – 11:00 Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems 11:00 – 11:25 My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey 11:30 – 12:00 Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing Key Highlights Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories A software factory is a standard, repeatable way for a team to build, test and release software. The speakers shared common mistakes to avoid and what actually worked when they built it at scale. Education An educator’s view on preparing the next generation of cloud engineers. What students should prepare before joining the industry, and how to close the gap between university and real work. AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture Lambda can now serve web requests over native HTTP and handle up to 128 requests at the same time in one function, which changes how we think about serverless web apps. No adapter layer is needed, and Active CPU Billing (paying only for the time the CPU is actually working) helps reduce cost. The session compared serverless with Docker on EC2/ECS using real performance benchmarks. Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems Modern systems need asynchronous processing (work is put in a queue and handled later) so that one slow part does not block the whole system. Amazon SQS (a managed message queue) helps decouple (separate) components and scale each part independently. Practical design patterns and tips, for example using a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) to keep messages that keep failing. My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey A former intern shared how they applied AWS services to a real project during 3 months. Lessons and advice for interns who are just starting. Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing How to make a first open source contribution from zero. How to build a habit of contributing regularly and stay motivated, and how this helps skills and career. Key Takeaways Serverless is not only for small functions anymore; it can be a real option for web applications, but the choice should be based on cost and performance data, not habit. Using a queue (SQS) between steps makes a system more reliable: if one step fails, messages wait in the queue instead of being lost. An internship is short. Learning steadily every day and building a real project matters more than reading a lot of theory. Applying to My Work Consider adding Amazon SQS between the upload step and the processing step (Lambda) in our team’s capstone workshop, with a DLQ for failed jobs. When choosing between Lambda and containers for the workshop, compare cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator before deciding. Follow the advice from the internship session: update my worklog honestly every week and practice labs instead of only reading. Event Experience This event was very close to my situation as an intern. The session from a former intern showed me what a 3-month internship can realistically achieve, and the Lambda and SQS sessions connected directly to services our team may use in the workshop. I also learned that contributing to open source is something I can start small with.

title: Blog 3
content:
Lambda, SQS and EventBridge now support payloads up to 1 MB Posted on: AWS Study Group VN (Facebook) – 06/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2328196167945342/
In event-driven architecture, services exchange data through a payload (the data attached to a message or event). The old limit was 256 KB, so large data such as LLM prompts, telemetry or ML output had to be split, compressed or stored in S3.
Since early 2026, AWS has raised the limit to 1 MB for:
AWS Lambda: asynchronous invocations Amazon SQS: all messages in queues Amazon EventBridge: all events on event buses The change applies automatically to existing and new resources, with nothing to enable. If you set the SQS MaximumMessageSize attribute yourself, or wrote chunking logic around the 256 KB threshold, you may need to adjust it.
Important notes from the article:
Lambda’s 15-minute timeout and memory limits are unchanged. Parsing large JSON can use more memory and time, so load test with realistic payloads Logging full payloads to CloudWatch Logs increases cost, so log selectively or sample Every consumer must be able to handle the larger payloads The claim check pattern (store large data in S3 and pass a reference) is still useful when payloads exceed 1 MB, when multiple consumers need the data, or when audit is required For a document flow such as S3, Lambda, Textract and Bedrock, this change lets you pass more context in one message without workarounds.
Source: More room to build: serverless services now support payloads up to 1 MB – Anton Aleksandrov, Debasis Rath, AWS Compute Blog (29/01/2026) https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/more-room-to-build-serverless-services-now-support-payloads-up-to-1-mb/
